title: How the Psalms work
hookLine: 150 songs of praise, anger, grief and trust, prayed by the Church every day

cards: Somewhere right now it's early morning, and a monk in a cold chapel is singing a psalm. Somewhere else it's evening, and a nurse on her break is reading one on her phone. A priest on a train prays one under his breath.
A grieving family hears one read at a funeral. Every single day, all over the world, the Church prays the same book of songs, around the clock.
It's the oldest prayer book Christians have, and Jesus prayed from it himself.

teach.b: The psalter is the Book of Psalms: a hundred and fifty songs. The word comes from Greek. A psalterion was a stringed instrument, and a psalm was a song sung to plucked strings.
In Hebrew the book is called Tehillim, praises. But here's the surprise: a great many aren't cheerful at all.
There are more psalms of complaint than of anything else: songs that ask God where he's gone, why the wicked win, how long this will last. Psalms of anger so raw they're hard to read aloud.
Psalms of grief, of guilt, of homesickness, of trust in the dark.

A fourth-century bishop, Athanasius of Alexandria, wrote that most of scripture speaks to you, but the psalms speak for you, like a mirror of your own heart. Whatever you're feeling, someone already prayed it.
The Douay-Rheims follows the old Greek and Latin Bibles, which divide a few psalms differently from the Hebrew, so for most of the book the Douay number is one lower than a modern Bible's.
The well-known shepherd psalm is Psalm 23 in most Bibles, and Psalm 22 in the Douay. On this path, the Hebrew number comes in brackets.
Catholics meet the psalms all the time: one is sung at every Mass between the readings, and the Liturgy of the Hours, the Church's daily prayer, walks through them morning, evening and night.
The book ends on one line: "Let every spirit praise the Lord. Alleluia."

how: Catholics hear a psalm sung or read at every Mass between the readings, and priests, religious and many lay people pray the psalms daily in the Liturgy of the Hours, at morning, evening and night.

o: a book of hymns written for Mass

games.q: what's inside the book — tap the pairs.
p: the shepherd psalm, 23 in most Bibles

s: the psalms are almost all happy songs of praise
complaints and laments are among the most common kinds.

games.q: you're furious at someone and can't find words to pray. where would the psalter send you?
o: nowhere: the psalms are only for calm moods.
to a psalm that says exactly how angry you are.
straight to a psalm of thanksgiving.
games.why: the psalter is full of angry and grieving prayers. Athanasius said the psalms speak for you: whatever you feel, someone already prayed it.

practice: If there's a Bible nearby, let it fall open near the middle, where the Psalms usually are, and read one verse; if not, pick any number from one to a hundred and fifty to look up later.
Then ask one honest question, what am I actually feeling today, tired, grateful, angry, worried, fine, and just name it. If you pray, hold that feeling up to God as it is.
